Analytical modeling of multiple borehole heat exchangers in layered soil with pile-soil thermal contact resistance
Estimating daily run-of-river hydropower generation from open hydrometeorological data: Limits of hydrology-based modelling
abstract: Hydropower is important for energy system modelling, where run-of-river hydropower is commonly represented as prescribed non-dispatchable generation. This study uses open hydrometeorological datasets to estimate the aggregated daily run-of-river generation and to assess the explanatory limits of hydrology-based modelling. ERA5, GEOGLOWS V2, and GloFAS v4.0 reanalyses are evaluated against reported generation for six European countries as a case study: France, Austria, Germany, Finland, Portugal, and Romania. Different input sets are compared within a consistent modelling framework, and the best-performing baseline model is used to diagnose remaining estimation errors. The results show that GloFAS river discharge provides the most suitable input for reproducing reported run-of-river generation, as it captures the dominant seasonal hydrological variability more robustly than the models with ERA5 and GEOGLOWS. The remaining error is the uncaptured short-term variation in reported generation. Additional tests indicate that accounting for reservoir generation provides limited improvements in model performance at the aggregated daily country level, while part of the residual is associated with electricity-price deviations, potentially reflecting short-term operation enabled by unclassified pondage within reported run-of-river generation. Accordingly, representing reported run-of-river generation as fully non-dispatchable in large-scale energy system models may overlook the potential short-term flexibility contained in the reported profiles The hydrology-based run-of-river estimates should therefore be interpreted as weather-dependent availability profiles, and the reproducible workflow in this study can produce such profiles for large-scale energy system studies across historical weather years beyond the period covered by reported data.

title: Balancing profit and exergy efficiency: Optimal dispatch strategies for integrated energy systems with high renewable penetration
How low-level jets impact the power curve of floating offshore wind turbines: Comprehensive analysis and prediction model
Assessment of the technical feasibility of pruning waste gasification in a pilot-scale downdraft plant
abstract: Pruning activities for the maintenance of electrical distribution lines in the city of Bogotá and peripheral municipalities produce tons of residues to be treated. This study aims to evaluate the technical feasibility of the valorisation route through gasification, evaluating the different particle size distributions, and the effect of operational conditions in a downdraft gasification process. A systematic homogenization and classification of biomass is conducted to define three size fractions, followed by the selection of the best mixture based on the angle of repose (AOR), using an adapted method with the Abrams cone. Statistical analyses (ANOVA and Tukey HSD’s test) revealed that a 70–30 wt.% mixture of intermediate and fine particles offers the most favourable flow characteristics. This mixture is used in a pilot-scale 20 kW downdraft gasifier to evaluate the effect of different equivalence ratios (ER) on the gasification performance. A low-cost and easy-to-implement analysis of the reactor temperature stability through Gaussian Mixture Modelling (GMM) is proposed, showing that the 70–30 wt.% mixture and an ER of 0.22 facilitate continuous feeding without blockages. The findings demonstrate that combining flowability analysis with thermal performance evaluation is a powerful tool to evaluate the performance of biomass gasification using heterogeneous feedstocks like pruning waste in real operative conditions, ultimately contributing to local bioenergy initiatives and sustainable waste valorisation strategies.

title: Optimizing China's offshore wind-solar power systems for supply–demand matching: exploring wind-solar and wind-solar-storage integration models
Experimental validation of a dynamic double-layer photovoltaic installation for enhanced energy production per unit of occupied land area
abstract: Large-scale photovoltaic deployment requires solutions that increase electricity production per unit of occupied land area. This study presents and validates through on-field tests a dynamic double-layer photovoltaic installation, consisting of two vertically stacked bifacial layers occupying the same land area of a conventional single-layer installation. The two stacked layers are capable of independent solar tracking. A custom-built scaled prototype with twelve rotating bifacial modules and independent current sensing was operated on field under three different operation modes and compared with a conventional single-layer installation occupying the same ground area. The most efficient operation mode, which has the top layer dynamically tracking the sun and the bottom layer fixed, achieved a gain of about +42% relative to a monofacial single-layer installation and +27% relative to a bifacial one, while a more simple open-loop tracking strategy based on a five-parameter sigmoid yielded gains close to +39% and +25% with negligible loss compared with closed-loop optimal control. The proposed installation is in principle agnostic with respect to the cell technology adopted and scalable from compact dynamic modules to utility-scale and agrivoltaic applications.

title: An innovative multiple substrates proportioning method for anaerobic co-digestion: from mechanism analysis to practical verification
Techno-economic optimization of a grid-connected community microgrid with net metering using metaheuristic algorithms
Engineering hierarchical microporous carbon with oxygen functionalization from enzymatic hydrolysis lignin for high-performance supercapacitors via Hydrothermal-KOH activation
Land-resource endowment and photovoltaic deployment in China
Transfer learning and convolutional neural networks for solar photovoltaic systems detection in distributed power grids
abstract: Accurate mapping and characterization of distributed solar photovoltaic (PV) systems are essential for energy planning, net demand forecasting, and policy-making. Traditional methods for collecting data on distributed electricity generation are often labor-intensive, costly, or impractical. This study leverages recent advances in machine learning, introducing state-of-the-art image segmentation architectures for automated PV panel detection from remotely sensed data. To address constraints in training time and dataset size, transfer learning is applied using pre-trained large-scale deep neural networks as feature extractors. Additionally, a novel hard example mining scheme is proposed to enhance detection accuracy. Through a comprehensive framework, factors influencing prediction accuracy, such as PV recognition thresholds, segmentation model architecture, sampling strategies, and encoder parameter freezing, are systematically examined. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms other models, achieving an F1 score above 0.91 and an IoU exceeding 0.83. This research advances automated infrastructure mapping, providing scalable solutions for monitoring distributed PV systems and offering transferable methodologies for broader applications.

Numerical modeling of aquifer-well interactions and energy performance in standing column well geothermal systems
abstract: Shallow geothermal energy represents a renewable, low-carbon resource for sustainable urban heating and cooling. Standing column wells exploit the hydraulic and thermal connection between a borehole and the surrounding formation to provide compact, high-capacity heat exchange from a single well. However, their performance is strongly controlled by subsurface hydraulic conditions and operating strategy. This study develops a coupled thermal-hydraulic numerical model of a standing column well system to investigate the subsurface effects. The model is validated against field thermal response test data and is then applied to a field case representative of the study area. A parametric analysis examines the effects of aquifer permeability, bleed ratio, well radius, reinjection temperature, and depth on thermal and hydraulic performance. The results reveal a permeability-dependent transition from conduction-supported to aquifer-supported operation. At low permeability, heat transfer is conductive unless bleed induces groundwater inflow. At high permeability, groundwater exchange increases thermal capacity and reverses the effects of well geometry. Larger wells favor conductive heat exchange, whereas smaller wells enhance aquifer inflow and thermal output. Greater depth provides modest benefits under conduction-supported conditions but substantially increases capacity under active aquifer exchange conditions. Bleed improves performance in both regimes, although the associated drawdown constrains operation. These trends persist over 120 days, with performance declines quantified. Thermal short-circuiting during upward flow through the riser reduces the temperature gain acquired in the annulus by approximately 9-13%. Therefore, standing column well design should consider aquifer-well connectivity, bleed operation, and well geometry.

title: Design and performance study of triple reflection solar concentrated photocatalytic nitrate reduction reactor
Plantwide dynamic optimization of a hybrid solar thermal power plant modeled using deep neural networks
Energy and economic performance evaluation of photovoltaic/thermal modules with serpentine and parallel flow channels: a comprehensive analysis
abstract: This study presents a comparative energy–economic assessment of water-based photovoltaic/thermal modules employing serpentine and parallel flow channels. Utilizing a bond graph methodology, a numerical model was developed to account for the thermal–hydraulic characteristics of the modules. Results demonstrate that the serpentine configuration significantly outperforms the parallel design. Under still-air conditions, the serpentine layout improves electrical, thermal, and net overall efficiencies by 2.2%, 13.7%, and 11.1%, respectively, with thermal improvements reaching 37.6% at higher wind speeds. Both configurations achieve optimal net efficiency at a water mass flux of 1000 kgs-1m-2, representing a critical balance between energy generation and pumping consumption. Economically, while photovoltaic/thermal modules generally incur higher payback periods than standalone photovoltaic module, the serpentine configuration achieves superior cost-competitiveness. At optimal flow and optimal channel row count, the serpentine system yields a levelized cost of energy up to 10% lower than a standalone photovoltaic module, whereas the parallel configuration incurs economic penalties due to elevated pumping requirements. Furthermore, implementing an intermediate pumping cut-off threshold effectively improves the economic performance in high mass flux scenarios. Overall, the proposed modeling framework offers a highly transferable approach for assessing and optimizing the energy and techno-economic performance of photovoltaic/thermal modules across varying climates.

title: Adaptive control of hybrid electrolyzer systems for coordinated frequency regulation and hydrogen production in low-inertia power networks
abstract: The increasing penetration of renewable energy sources has introduced considerable frequency instability in low-inertia power networks, highlighting the need for flexible and fast-acting frequency regulation solutions. This paper proposes a hybrid electrolyzer (HE) system featuring dual-mode operation for both frequency regulation (FR) and hydrogen production (HP). The system integrates a fast-response proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzer with a cost-effective alkaline (AL) electrolyzer, coordinated through an adaptive control strategy coupled with an electricity price-responsive mechanism. The proposed approach enhances both frequency quality and hydrogen yield while accounting for the dynamic characteristics and operational constraints of the electrolyzers. The study further examines the interaction between frequency regulation and hydrogen production, revealing that power sharing ratios and setpoint flexibility critically influence system economics, frequency reserves, and HP capacity. In addition, a hybrid optimization technique is employed to tune the proportional–integral (PI) controller gains of the DC–DC converter, ensuring stable active power control of the HE system. Simulations are conducted across three test systems to validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves frequency stability and hydrogen generation while achieving notable economic advantages over conventional single-electrolyzer-based systems.

title: From waste to wealth: Optimizing biogas plants for the energy transition
Inertial effects on the mechanical efficiency of a semi-passive oscillating hydrofoil energy harvester
abstract: Oscillating-foil-based energy harvesters have demonstrated strong potential for low-speed hydrokinetic energy extraction; however, the actuator-level mechanical energy balance associated with prescribed pitching motion remains poorly understood. The present work experimentally characterizes how foil mass ratio, pitching-axis location, and reduced frequency jointly govern the hydrodynamic and mechanical efficiencies of a semi-passive oscillating hydrofoil. Results show that rotational inertia redistributes actuator demand through phase-dependent torque exchange, while heave-pitch coupling can partially cancel this demand when favorably phased. Pitching-axis location modifies the phase and direction of the fluid torque through changes in the effective hydrodynamic moment arm. Reduced frequency governs the balance between enhanced unsteady loading and inertia-amplified actuator demand. Optimal performance is achieved within reduced frequency region of 0.125-0.16 using quarter-chord to one-third-chord pitching axes and relatively low foil mass ratios from about 0.5 to 2.0, yielding a peak mechanical efficiency of 33.96% -- which can diverge from the hydrodynamic efficiency by approximately 38.16% depending on configuration. Torque-loop analysis and PIV measurements show that this synchronization is a key mechanism governing the observed efficiency trends.

title: Efficient biomass pyrolysis under sub-design solar input through SiC foam integration and process parameter optimization
abstract: Solar thermochemical reactors often operate below their design power because solar irradiance varies. This study evaluates whether silicon carbide (SiC) foam can extend the effective operating window of a solar-driven packed-bed biomass pyrolysis reactor under sub-design input. A Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) framework coupled a one-dimensional shrinking-core particle model with a semi-detailed kinetic model (SDKM). The model was applied to a 5 kW prototype by varying the peak incident radiative flux densities ( I ) from 1.24 to 2.49 MW∙m −2 (40–80% of the design power), SiC foam porosity ( ϕ SiC ), and nominal residence time ( NRT ). At ϕ SiC = 0.9 and NRT = 15 s, essentially complete biomass pyrolysis was achieved at I = 1.55 MW∙m −2 , corresponding to only 50% of the design power, and the oil fraction reached 45%. Above this threshold, additional input mainly intensified PLPS decomposition and oil cracking rather than biomass conversion. Direct comparison with a bed without foam showed that SiC foam increased the conversion rate from 29% to as high as 79%. At ϕ SiC = 0.94, the axial temperature difference decreased from 1018 to 347 K, and the effective conversion rate reached 73%. Increasing NRT from 15 to 120 s increased oil-to-gas conversion by 150% with little change in bed temperature. These results quantify the extension of the reactor operating window enabled by SiC foam and clarify the distinct effects of radiative input and NRT on product distribution.

title: Integrating Gaussian splatting and machine learning for solar analysis in sustainable buildings
abstract: This study presents a geometry-aware framework for residential solar energy estimation that integrates unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based photogrammetry, three-dimensional Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), physics-based energy modeling, and multimodal machine learning (ML) for active and passive solar prediction. Building geometries are reconstructed from low-cost UAV video using segment anything model 3 (SAM 3) segmentation, structure-from-motion, and dense reconstruction, with 3DGS generating scene representations that preserve roof and facade features relevant to solar analysis, converted into watertight level of detail 3 (LOD3) building envelopes with integrated fenestration and transformed into EnergyPlus-compatible energy models at five performance levels. Validation across 33 residential buildings confirms good agreement between reconstructed and ground-truth dimensions and realistic thermal energy demand trends. Solar simulations evaluate annual photovoltaic (PV) potential, sunlit area, and internal solar gains, and a multimodal graph neural network (GNN) jointly processing geometry-aware and scalar building features for rapid, simulation-free estimation, achieving testing R 2 values of 0.890, 0.753, and 0.815 for annual internal solar gain, PV generation, and total sunlit area, respectively. The results demonstrate the potential of geometry-aware scene representations and machine learning as a scalable approach for rapid solar-performance assessment.

title: Simple radial translation of sub dishes for enhanced concentration ratio and flux uniformity in multi-dish solar concentrators
A dimensionless framework for predicting thermal recovery efficiency in HT-ATES under coupled buoyancy and ambient groundwater flow

A methodology for selecting phase transition models in solid/liquid phase change materials
abstract: Phase change materials play a critical role in latent heat thermal energy storage and thermal management systems due to their ability to absorb and release large amounts of heat during quasi-isothermal phase transitions. Accurate modelling of their thermophysical properties is essential for the optimal design and performance assessment of such systems. This study presents a systematic methodology for identifying the most reliable mathematical model to describe phase transition in a given material. First, a comprehensive review of modelling approaches was conducted. In addition, a classification of the existing models is proposed based on their underlying mathematical characteristics. Then, a benchmarking process is presented, which comprises three steps, a visual comparison of the experimental data and model outputs, numerical performance evaluation through the normalised root-mean-square error, and statistical assessment via the Taylor diagram. The performance of these models was evaluated by comparing their numerical estimations of enthalpy and apparent heat capacity against experimental data obtained for sodium nitrate. The selection of this particular PCM was associated with the ongoing research of the authors on high-temperature PCM-based TES systems. Experimental data were acquired using a differential scanning calorimeter within the temperature range of 285-330 °C, with a heating rate of 1 K/min, and employing isothermal periods of 10 minutes. The results revealed significant differences in model accuracy, offering valuable insights for selecting appropriate models for specific material. Utilising the concept of normalised root mean squared error, the Gumbel model demonstrated superior adjustment for apparent heat capacity, whereas the triangular model exhibited a more accurate fit for the enthalpy function of sodium nitrate, with errors of 26% and 17%, respectively. Based on the Taylor diagram, the Gumbel model was selected to represent the phase transition of sodium nitrate due to its high accuracy, evidenced by an error margin of less than 25%, and its strong correlation coefficient exceeding 0.95. This study not only enhances the understanding of modelling thermal properties in phase transition but also guides future research and development in this field. The proposed selection procedure can be effectively replicated to model the phase transition of various phase change materials commonly utilised in industrial applications, because its fundamentals are based on the mathematical principles of phase transition. Consequently, it can be applied to other materials, regardless of their melting temperature.

Comparison of mounting systems in utility-scale photovoltaic installations: Analysis of land occupation
abstract: Utility-scale photovoltaic installations require substantial land areas. This study investigates the land area required for utility-scale photovoltaic installations as a function of the photovoltaic module mounting system employed. The study focuses on the photovoltaic field; therefore, roads, substations, service buildings and other related infrastructure are excluded. To examine the influence of geographic location on utility-scale photovoltaic systems design and performance, 18 sites across both hemispheres were analysed. Four representative mounting configurations were evaluated: 2 V × 15 and 3 V × 10 (fixed tilt angle systems), and 1 V × 60 and 2 V × 30 (horizontal single-axis trackers). The analysis process was predicated upon four assessment indicators, namely land use intensity, power density, energy density, and ground coverage ratio. A detailed analysis leads to several conclusions. Fixed-tilt systems show strong latitude dependence due to variations in optimal tilt angle, whereas horizontal single-axis trackers are largely insensitive to latitude except at high latitudes. The 2 V × 30 configuration provides the best performance across both hemispheres based on four indicators. For fixed-tilt systems, the 3 V × 10 configuration is the best. As a general tendency, configurations with more vertically stacked modules per row tend to achieve superior performance.

title: Numerical investigation of heat extraction performance of a multi-casing coaxial well with multilateral branches for enhanced geothermal systems
abstract: A novel enhanced geothermal system is proposed using a multi-casing coaxial well with multilateral branches, where a single main wellbore with three concentric pipes separates the injection zone from two production zones. This configuration creates two independent production zones, significantly expanding the heat exchange volume and improving overall heat extraction efficiency. A three-dimensional fully coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical numerical model was established to systematically simulate the heat extraction performance of the newly proposed system and compare it with a conventional Enhanced Geothermal System using a single-casing coaxial well with multilateral branches. The results show that the cumulative power of the newly proposed system increases by approximately 14%-52% compared to the conventional one under different fracture densities over a 60-year operation period. The pressure difference between the injection well and production well decreases by 81%-94%. Parametric analysis reveals that heat extraction efficiency is further improved by controlling the fracture dimensions, selecting an appropriate number of branches, maximizing the length of the branches, and adjusting the injection rate. Furthermore, economic analysis shows that the newly proposed system can significantly reduce the levelized cost of energy compared with conventional systems. This research proposes an alternative enhanced geothermal design that significantly improves heat extraction performance.

Thermoresponsive building envelope with optical modulation and latent heat storage: Energy savings and thermal comfort evaluation under diverse climatic conditions
abstract: Thermal comfort is essential for occupant well-being, yet maintaining it consumes a substantial portion of building energy. To address this, this study proposes and fabricates an innovative thermoresponsive building envelope integrating a thermoresponsive hydrogel (TH) layer with a phase change material (PCM) layer. The TH enables optical modulation, adjusting solar absorption and reflection with temperature to reduce solar radiation during hot seasons while capturing solar heat during cold seasons. Simultaneously, the PCM provides latent heat storage, reducing daily temperature fluctuations and maintaining nighttime indoor temperatures during cold seasons, thereby lowering heating demand and improving thermal comfort. Sensitivity analysis indicated that the optimal transition temperature of the TH layer is higher in the colder regions due to greater heating demand and lower ambient temperatures, whereas the optimal phase change temperature of the PCM layer lies below the heating setpoint to compensate for the heating reduction. Based on typical meteorological year weather data, simulations across 34 provincial-level capital cities of China demonstrated that the proposed envelope can reduce annual energy consumption by 4.0-18.2% (7.8-17.1 MJ m -2 ) and increase comfort hours by 0.2-9.7% compared to a bare envelope in residential buildings with heating and cooling setpoints of 20 °C and 26 °C, respectively, depending on the region and the optimal transition temperatures of both the TH and PCM layers. These results highlight the feasibility of passive building envelope designs as an effective energy-saving and thermal comfort strategy across different climates.

title: Combined disposal of water treatment and sewage sludge within the water municipal system
abstract: This study investigated the mesophilic anaerobic co-digestion of sewage sludge (SS) and water treatment sludge (WTS) as an integrated strategy for sludge management and renewable energy recovery in municipal water and wastewater systems. Batch respirometric tests were conducted at 35 ± 1 °C using SS–WTS mixtures prepared on the basis of volatile solids (VS), with WTS doses ranging from 0.1 to 1.0 g VS per 1.0 g VS of SS. The effect of WTS addition was evaluated through unit biogas production, specific methanogenic activity (SMA), and physicochemical characterization of both sludge types. The results showed that WTS influenced anaerobic digestion in a strongly dose-dependent manner. The highest process efficiency was obtained at 0.3 g VS WTS per 1.0 g VS SS, where biogas production increased by up to 50% and methanogenic activity by up to 35% compared with SS digestion alone. Higher WTS doses reduced fermentation efficiency, most likely due to the increasing contribution of mineral components, including aluminium- and iron-rich phases. The findings indicate that WTS should not be considered a conventional energy-rich co-substrate, but rather a mineral conditioning component that can improve anaerobic digestion only within an optimized dosage range. The proposed SS–WTS co-digestion approach may support sustainable sludge valorization, enhanced biogas recovery, and circular management of residues generated in municipal water systems.

A soft-linking approach to couple urban microclimate analysis and renewable integration in energy district planning
abstract: ABSTRACT Rapid urbanisation and climate change are intensifying urban overheating, energy demand, and greenhouse gas emissions, highlighting the need for strategies that jointly address microclimate mitigation and energy system decarbonisation. However, passive urban design measures and active energy solutions are often assessed independently, limiting the understanding of their combined effects at the district scale. This study develops and applies a multi-scale sequential soft-linking to assess how outdoor microclimatic conditions affect building thermal demand and, subsequently, district energy system performance in urban regeneration contexts.. The approach connects ENVI-met, EnergyPlus, and EnergyPLAN, enabling the transfer of microclimatic boundary conditions into dynamic building simulations and the resulting demand profiles to district-level energy modelling. The framework supports the coordinated assessment of nature-based solutions, envelope retrofitting, and renewable-based energy systems. The methodology is applied to a Mediterranean residential district through four scenarios (reference, passive-only, active-only, and integrated) evaluated using environmental, energy, and economic indicators. Results show that passive measures reduce thermal loads and improve outdoor comfort, while active solutions enhance renewable penetration and system flexibility. The combined passive–active scenario achivesprimary energy reductions of about 60% and CO 2 emission cuts up to 75-80%, while mitigating peak summer thermal stress and supporting climate-responsive, low-carbon urban district planning.

Dark fermentation of chicken manure and citrus wastewater for renewable biohydrogen production: The role of microbial functional balance
abstract: ABSTRACT Dark fermentation of chicken manure waste and citrus wastewater was evaluated as a strategy to enhance biohydrogen production from agro-industrial residues. Eight batch assays using autochthonous and allochthonous inocula were conducted to assess hydrogen production, metabolite profiles, and microbial community dynamics under different substrate and inoculum configurations. The highest cumulative H 2 production reached 2774 mL H 2 L -1 , corresponding to 0.186 L H 2 g -1 VS added, with faster kinetics and reduced lag phases in the best-performing assays. The observed hydrogen performance was consistent with the established importance of metabolic pathway selection and electron partitioning in mixed culture dark fermentation. High performing systems were characterized by acetate–butyrate fermentation, whereas propionate and C1-related pathways were associated with reduced or delayed hydrogen production. Metagenomic analysis revealed enrichment of hydrogenogenic KEGG Orthologs associated with pyruvate oxidation and [FeFe]-hydrogenases in high-performing reactors. Enhanced hydrogen production was linked to functionally complementary microbial consortia involving hydrolytic and fermentative genera, particularly Bacteroides, Clostridium , and Caldicoprobacter . Overall, the results are consistent with previous evidence highlighting the importance of microbial functional organization and metabolic pathway distribution in determining hydrogen production from mixed agro-industrial substrates, providing mechanistic insights for the optimization of dark fermentation systems.

abstract: This work compares two bifacial photovoltaic configurations for irrigation across different latitudes: Vertical panels and a gabled-roof arrangement, both aligned along a north–south axis, with their front sides facing east and west, considering both water volume-to-energy productivity (m 3 /kWh) and annual specific pumped volume (m 3 /kWp per year). Photovoltaic generation was simulated in the software tool PVsyst tapping Typical Meteorological Year data for Low (27.89 °N), Mid (39.50 °N), and High (52.55 °N) latitudes. Pumped flow was estimated as a function of power using a polynomial model with a single pump to two pumps in parallel switching rule. In terms of annual specific energy yield, the vertical configuration outperformed the gabled counterpart by 5.4%, 14.7%, and 13.7%, while in terms of annual specific pumped volume the vertical outperformance was of 4.0%, 7.5%, and 9.0%, for the Low, Mid, and High latitude, respectively. Although the gabled-roof configuration achieved slightly higher water volume-to-energy productivity, the vertical configuration delivered more total annual pumped volume due to its higher integrated energy yield. A ±20% sensitivity analysis on the pump-switching power threshold confirmed the robustness of these results. As a takeaway, vertical bifacial PV is more effective for maximizing annual irrigation water delivery across the latitudes considered.

Coupled effects of atmospheric stability and terrain slope on wind turbine wake evolution and downstream power performance over hilly terrain
abstract: The rapid deployment of onshore wind farms in complex terrain is an important pathway for expanding wind energy deployment. However, the coupled effects of atmospheric stability and terrain slope on wind turbine wake evolution and downstream power performance remain insufficiently understood, hindering accurate energy-yield assessment and effective wind-farm layout optimization. In this study, high-fidelity large-eddy simulations are conducted to investigate turbine wakes over flat terrain, a gentle hill, and a steep hill under convective, neutral, and stable atmospheric conditions. The results demonstrate that wake evolution and downstream power performance are jointly controlled by atmospheric stability, terrain slope, and upstream turbine wakes. Coriolis-induced wind veer and terrain-induced flow distortion lead to three-dimensional wake deflection, which becomes more pronounced with increasing atmospheric stability and terrain slope. Under stable conditions over the steep hill, the downstream distributions of power loss and power variability exhibit pronounced asymmetry, together with faster power recovery. Momentum-flux analysis shows that this accelerated recovery is primarily driven by downward mean advective transport from the low-level jet rather than by enhanced turbulent mixing. Terrain-induced power loss and variability increase with terrain slope because of intensified flow separation on the leeward side. In contrast, the power loss and variability caused by upstream turbine wakes decrease over steeper terrain because the increased elevation difference reduces direct wake impingement on the downstream rotor. These findings clarify the coupled terrain–stability mechanisms governing wind turbine wakes and provide guidance for energy-yield assessment and turbine layout optimization in complex terrain.

Reducing hoary bat mortality using curtailment: Potential impacts to wind energy generation and value in the contiguous United States
abstract: : Mitigating wildlife impacts of wind energy involves power generation and conservation trade-offs. For bats, curtailing wind turbines reduces collision risk. Although curtailment is generally implemented during a narrow set of conditions (e.g., at night in late summer when wind speeds are relatively low), the impact on power production and revenue can be substantial at some wind energy facilities. Several studies have documented significant reductions in bat fatalities when wind turbines are curtailed, but few assess the energetic and economic costs. We modeled 12 curtailment scenarios using 3 cut-in speeds (5.0, 6.0, and 6.9 meters/second) and 4 seasons to assess the reduction in energy generation and energy value. Three of the curtailment periods were based on time periods curtailment has historically been tested or implemented. The fourth, based on when most hoary bat fatalities occur, was included to examine whether regionally specific data could reduce impacts to the wind industry. The median reduction in annual energy production was between 0.18% and 2.9%, with most scenarios involving a reduction of less than 1%. The median reduction in annual energy value was below 2% in most scenarios but was nearly 4.8% in the scenario with highest level of curtailment. Cut-in speed had a greater effect than seasonal duration, for both energy production and value, but the duration of the season moderated some of the impact of higher cut-in speeds. Given the conservation value increases with higher cut-in speeds, implementing curtailment based on regional, or even local, data could benefit bats, wind energy generation, and grid reliability.

Sonochemical engineering of Ag-Ni loaded ZnIn2S4 nanocomposites for enhanced solar-driven hydrogen evolution
abstract: The development of efficient photocatalytic routes for hydrogen production is of growing interest for sustainable energy conversion and the storage of renewable energy in the form of a chemical energy carrier. In this work, ZnIn 2 S 4 -based photocatalysts were engineered through the loading of commercial Ni nanoparticles (NPs) and the in-situ formation of Ag NPs via a sonochemical process, leading to enhanced photocatalytic performance. Among the synthesized photocatalysts, ZIS/AgNi-10 (10 min of sonication) exhibited the highest hydrogen evolution activity, reaching a value of 1.65 ± 0.04 mmol g -1 h -1 and apparent quantum efficiency (AQE) of 9.4 % at 420 nm. This improvement is attributed to the synergistic effect of Ni and Ag loading, where Ni provides active catalytic sites, while Ag NPs promote plasmon resonance and facilitate charge separation. These effects result in improved charge carrier dynamics and enhanced light absorption, as supported by optical and electrochemical analyses. Although a reduction in specific surface area is observed after sonication, this limitation is offset by the improved electronic and optical properties. Structural and compositional characterization further confirmed the effective integration of both components, inducing modulation of the electronic structure, including bandgap tuning and a shift in the valence band position. Overall, this work presents a simple, green and scalable strategy to optimize ZIS-based photocatalysts toward sustainable hydrogen generation and photon-to-chemical conversion, with relevance to renewable hydrogen technologies.

title: How increasing green hydrogen blending affects techno-economic and environmental performance of renewable energy communities across Italian climates
abstract: Renewable Energy Communities (RECs) can support the decarbonization of local energy systems by promoting renewable generation and sector coupling. This study evaluates the effect of increasing the hydrogen blending ratio from 10% to 20% by volume within an already hydrogen-integrated REC framework. Twelve scenarios are analysed across three Italian climatic zones-Reggio Calabria, Rome, and Turin-considering Combined Heat and Power (CHP) and Gas Absorption Heat Pump (GAHP) configurations coupled with photovoltaic generation, hydrogen production and storage, and hydrogen-natural gas blending. Results show that the response to higher hydrogen blending strongly depends on climate, thermal demand, and system architecture. Moving from 10% to 20% H 2 generally improves renewable-energy utilization and economic and environmental performance within the hydrogen-integrated configurations. The lowest Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE), 148.5 €/MWh, is obtained for the GAHP configuration in Reggio Calabria at 20% H 2 , with a Carbon Avoidance Cost (CAC) of 892.8 €/tCO 2 . CHP systems benefit more from high and sustained thermal demand, resulting in stronger thermal-electric coupling in colder climates. A trade-off also emerges: increasing the H 2 blending ratio can reduce the Self-Consumption Ratio (SCR) and Self-Sufficiency Ratio (SSR), because the additional PV generation required to support electrolysis also increases grid exports, while LCOE, CAC, and renewable-energy utilization improve. Comparisons with the conventional reference case are used to assess the overall PV-hydrogen-CHP/GAHP architecture and are not attributed to hydrogen blending alone. Sensitivity analysis shows that electricity and natural-gas prices and district-heating infrastructure costs dominate economic performance, whereas ±50% variations in hydrogen-component CAPEX have comparatively limited effects.

title: Nanostructured colored radiative cooling for energy-efficient buildings and thermal management applications
Experimental evaluation of planar heat pipes with active cooling integration for photovoltaic thermal hot-spot mitigation
abstract: Photovoltaic module efficiency declines at high operating temperature, while localized hot spots accelerate degradation, and may reduce module lifetime. This study develops and experimentally evaluates planar heat pipes intended for rear surface heat spreading and for feeding a compact active water-cooled sink. Five full-scale prototypes with different internal configurations were fabricated from stainless steel and tested in a fully automated test rig under non-uniform heating conditions. Experiments were conducted at heating-pad setpoints between 50 and 100 °C, inclination angles of 30° to 45°, and under both natural-convection and localized active water-cooling conditions. Under natural convection, the transferred heat was comparable to that of the reference case without planar heat pipes, indicating limited benefit in bulk heat removal. When coupled to the water-cooled sink, heat removal increased by approximately 15-25 percent relative to the non-cooled baseline. The principal benefit of the planar heat pipes was temperature homogenization, which reduced peak surface temperatures by approximately 8 to 32 °C, depending on the prototype configuration and operating conditions, while markedly suppressing thermal hot spots. To illustrate the potential impact on photovoltaic performance, the experimentally observed temperature reductions were evaluated using a simplified temperature-dependent PV model and representative meteorological data for Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The assessment indicated potential improvements in annual electricity production under the investigated assumptions. The results demonstrate that planar heat pipes are effective thermal spreaders for photovoltaic applications, particularly for reducing temperature gradients and mitigating hot-spot formation.

title: Thermodynamic characteristics and off-design performance of a direct heated supercritical CO2 Brayton cycle driven by solar-biomass complementarity
Measuring renewable energy droughts – A standardized framework for quantifying the “Dunkelflaute”
abstract: Securing the electricity supply during renewable energy droughts (German: Dunkelflauten) constitutes a major challenge to the process renewable energy transition. However, the lack of a consistent approach to measuring renewable energy droughts, or Dunkelflauten has limited our ability to understand the magnitude of the problem and develop specific policy recommendations. This study proposes a standardized approach to quantify renewable energy (RE) droughts in direct reference to the installed capacity and the overbuilding of renewable energies using the German renewable electricity market as a case in point. The analysis identifies annual, prolonged RE droughts lasting up to 11 days, mainly during winter months, with generation deficits of up to 50 GW. Smaller scale RE droughts are relatively frequent, posing charging challenges for potential storage systems. Our results point to the need for increased renewables capacity, more favorable conditions for the integration of additional (renewable) gas-fired backup power plants, and other long-term storage solutions. Together with a push for grid expansion and Demand Side Management (DSM) measures major system upgrades are needed to ensure security of supply particularly during winter months.

Renewable energy and storage systems for net/nearly zero energy buildings integrating electric vehicles with correlated stochastic charging: Uncertainty-aware multi-objective optimization and dynamic analysis
abstract: Integrating electric vehicles (EVs) with net/nearly zero energy buildings (NZEBs) is crucial for advancing sustainable, resilient, and low-carbon energy infrastructures. However, this integration introduces additional complexity and uncertainty due to the unpredictable nature of EV charging behaviors, which further complicates system design. This study proposes a multi-objective optimization approach for designing renewable energy systems (RESs) in NZEBs, accounting for stochastic EV charging behaviors and uncertainty correlations. By employing a multivariate copula model, this study effectively captured the dependence structures in EV charging events, preserving the inherent complexity and correlations of EV behaviors. The simulation results demonstrated that the designed RESs performed reliably under uncertain conditions, with average metrics for net interaction level, self-sufficiency ratio, and carbon dioxide emission reduction of 113.4%, 66.8%, and 45,280.0 kg, respectively. These results validated the effectiveness and feasibility of the designed RESs. The study advances the integration of EVs with NZEBs to enhance the resilience and sustainability of building energy systems, and provides practical insights for developing energy-efficient, low-carbon NZEBs in real-world applications.

Renewable district heating systems in rural areas considering seasonal storage and decreasing use of biomass
abstract: In rural areas, renewable heating networks can immediately achieve carbon-neutral heat supply. Such networks with a high proportion of biomass are already well established. However, these systems are not a universal solution due to future biomass competition and sustainability constraints. While previous studies mainly focus on retrofitting existing networks, this study addresses the techno-economic optimization of newly planned rural heating networks with progressively reduced biomass use. Six system combinations are modeled in TRNSYS and optimized using SciPy for heat demands of 2, 4 and 8 GWh/a and heat densities of 250, 500 and 750 kWh/m a, considering both subsidized and non-subsidized cases. The results show that biomass can be avoided in summer using solar thermal energy or PV-driven heat pumps at 10%–20% higher LCoH. Fully biomass-free systems increase costs by around 50% for low-demand cases, while seasonal pit thermal energy storage enables > 80% solar heat shares for high-demand networks at > 20% higher costs than biomass-based systems. German subsidies reduce LCoH by approximately 18% while having only a marginal influence on system sizing. Furthermore, heat density has a stronger influence on costs than demand scaling.

title: Wave power extraction by a circular-sector oscillating water column attached to a coastal corner
A systematic methodology for PTO sizing and hydrodynamic optimization of OWC systems in high-energy Atlantic environments
abstract: This study presents a systematic methodology for the hydrodynamic optimization and power take-off sizing of an L-shaped oscillating water column wave energy converter for high-energy Atlantic environments. While standard oscillating water column designs, such as the Mutriku wave power plant (18.5 kW per unit), serve as a global benchmark, this research demonstrates that such configurations lead to significant energy underutilization in more energetic sea states. The proposed methodology combines multi-criteria site assessment, hydrodynamic resonance tuning, and time-domain numerical simulations. It is validated through a case study on Tenerife (Canary Islands, Spain), where an optimal chamber geometry was identified, matching the dominant wave period (T p = 12.5 s). A key contribution of this work is the optimization of the power take-off capacity. Sensitivity analysis revealed that increasing the rated power to 60 kW effectively mitigates clipping losses, increasing the annual energy production by 105.66% to 138.48 MWh/year compared with the 18.5 kW reference. Furthermore, the capture width ratio improved from 12.16% to 22.51%, highlighting the importance of hydrodynamic–pneumatic impedance matching. Comparative results show that the Tenerife site is 60.61% more energetic than the Mutriku wave power plant, achieving 2308 full-load hours and a capacity factor of 26.45%. These findings provide a transferable engineering methodology for designing resource-optimized oscillating water column systems in high-energy coastal environments. • Systematic four-stage framework for OWC design and PTO optimization. • Hydrodynamic resonance maximized through chamber geometry tuning. • PTO sizing mitigates clipping losses in energetic wave environments. • Optimized PTO increases annual energy production. • Framework transferable to high-energy breakwater-integrated OWC systems.

title: Dynamic stall behaviors of the IEA 15 MW blade controlled by the passive vortex generators
A lumped-parameters dynamic model for metal hydride hydrogen storage in renewable energy systems
abstract: This study presents a zero-dimensional dynamic model for simulating a metal hydride hydrogen storage system integrated into renewable energy applications. The model is developed in MATLAB and subsequently integrated into TRNSYS to perform one-year dynamic simulations. The aim of this work is to provide an efficient and reliable simulation tool for hydrogen-based energy systems. The considered hydrogen storage system includes a cylindrical metal hydride tank filled with LaNi 5 alloy. The tank is integrated with an alkaline electrolyzer that produces the hydrogen to be stored and a high-temperature proton exchange membrane fuel cell that uses the hydrogen released from storage. The model simulates hydrogen absorption and desorption under different operating conditions. It is based on a set of ordinary differential equations representing the mass and energy balances, obtained by simplifying partial differential equations to reduce computational effort. The main novelty lies in integrating the metal hydride hydrogen storage with the high-temperature proton exchange membrane fuel cell, using its heat for hydrogen desorption. The model also includes a suitable heat transfer model based on the logarithmic mean temperature difference. Validation against experimental and numerical data shows excellent agreement, with percentage errors below 5%. The investigated system achieves a primary energy saving of 58% and a payback period of approximately 8 years.

Unlocking bioenergy from municipal organic waste via anaerobic digestion in off-grid coastal communities of low-resource regions
abstract: Increasing municipal solid waste generation, projected to exceed 3.8 billion tons annually by 2050, calls for biomass valorization beyond conventional disposal. This study evaluates anaerobic digestion (AD) of the organic fraction of municipal solid waste (OFMSW) as a decentralized waste-to-energy solution for isolated coastal communities in developing countries. Compositional and physicochemical characterization of locally generated OFMSW revealed high biodegradable organic content and favorable parameters for AD. Biomethane potential (BMP) was assessed at inoculum-to-substrate ratios (ISR) of 1.0–2.5 under mesophilic conditions (35 °C) without mechanical mixing. ISR 2.5 achieved the highest yield (455 mL CH 4 g -1 VS), with production stabilizing within 17 days. These conditions informed subsequent semi-continuous operation using solid swine manure (SM) as inoculum at an organic loading rate (OLR) of 1.08 g VS L -1 day -1 . The reactors maintained stable performance without mechanical mixing or external alkalinity addition, producing 0.53 NL biogas g -1 VS at steady state, with pH of 6.4–6.8 and VFA-to-alkalinity ratios below 0.3. Community-scale energy balance and sensitivity analyses indicated that projected biogas production could replace 17.67–69.51% of local liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) demand, yielding estimated fuel-cost savings of USD 552–2,171; the departmental reference scenario yielded 29.54% substitution and USD 923 in savings. By integrating local feedstock characteristics, experimental digestion performance, and scenario-based energy substitution, this study provides evidence for decentralized bioenergy assessment and potential deployment in resource-constrained coastal communities, consistent with recovery priorities within the waste hierarchy.

Mechanistic insights into N2O abatement over SFCMO-based direct ammonia solid oxide fuel cell: polarization behavior and environmental application
abstract: Solid-oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) are investigated for N 2 O abatement, targeting the decomposition of this potent greenhouse gas while generating electricity as by-product. Although O 2 is typically the oxidant in SOFCs, N 2 O can also serve this role, as N 2 O decomposes into N 2 and O 2 under operating conditions. This work analyzes a double-perovskite Sr 2 Fe 1.45 Co 0.05 Mo 0.5 O 6− δ (SFCMO) as a cathode for N 2 O reduction. Dilatometry indicated an average thermal expansion coefficient of 10.7 x 10 -6 °C -1 , compatible with common SOFC electrolytes. The SFCMO|GDC|YSZ|Ni-YSZ cell was tested with O 2 or N 2 O, while the anode was fueled with NH 3 . Electrochemical characterization of the cell was performed via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and distribution function of relaxation times (DFRT) between 600 – 750 °C. Analysis indicated that surface exchange was the rate-limiting step of the oxygen reduction reaction. N 2 O as a source of oxygen atoms, which effectively lowers the oxygen partial pressure ( ) at the cathode, may increase the concentration of oxygen vacancies and enhance surface redox activity. Accordingly, the cell supplied with N 2 O exhibited more than a 30 % increase in power density compared to operation with O 2 , with an average N 2 O conversion of ∼41.7 %. These findings demonstrate SFCMO electrode as an efficient electrocatalyst for N 2 O abatement for intermediate-temperature SOFCs fueled by ammonia.

Mediterranean offshore wind spatial potential: Focusing on national targets of Italy, Greece and Cyprus for electricity and hydrogen production
abstract: Offshore wind and green hydrogen are expected to play a central role in Mediterranean decarbonisation, yet deep waters, intense coastal uses, and visual-acceptance constraints make siting and system design challenging. This study develops an integrated geospatial and techno-economic framework that combines marine spatial-planning layers, long-term wind reanalysis, offshore wind-farm design, and power-to-x valuation to assess where offshore wind can support electricity supply and hydrogen production. Spatial exclusions, bathymetric limits, and a visual-impact index reduce the basin to about 6.6 ⋅ 1 0 5 km 2 of eligible sea space (about 24% of the Mediterranean). For each grid cell, multi-year wind series are coupled with precomputed performance and cost tables for fixed-bottom and floating concepts, multiple turbine ratings, layouts, and spacings, producing spatially resolved indicators for annual electricity yield and levelised costs for electricity and hydrogen. For Italy, Greece, and Cyprus, 2030 electricity and hydrogen targets can be met using less than 8% of the eligible area, while export-oriented 2050 cases require up to about 55% in Italy and 75% in Greece and Cyprus, with avoided emissions on the order of several tens of MtCO 2 yr −1 .

Direct electrification and hydrogen-based pathways in EU passenger transport: Energy, environmental, and material implications
abstract: ABSTRACT Hydrogen-based passenger transport pathways are increasingly considered as potential decarbonization options in the European Union’s (EU) energy transition, particularly for long-distance and high-utilization applications where direct electrification may face operational constraints. However, their representation in Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs) and their system-wide energy, environmental, and material implications remain insufficiently assessed. This study extends the IAM WILIAM by incorporating hydrogen-based passenger transport pathways for light-duty vehicles, buses, and rail, together with electrolytic hydrogen production, storage, distribution, refueling infrastructure, greenhouse gas (GHG) and pollutant emissions, and critical material requirements. We assess EU policy-aligned scenarios focused on passenger transport, combining direct electrification, fuel cell electric vehicle (FCEV) deployment, renewable electricity expansion, and demand-side sufficiency assumptions. Results show that direct electrification plays the central role in reducing liquid fuel demand, primary energy (PE) consumption, and GHG and pollutant emissions. Adding hydrogen-based pathways further reduces liquid fuel demand and several emissions, especially VOC, CO, and CO 2 , but delivers smaller additional reductions than direct electrification alone and negligible additional reductions for CH 4 . In the most hydrogen-intensive scenario, FCEV deployment requires 137 GW of electrolyzer capacity, 44200 refuelling stations, and up to 196 GW of additional electricity generation capacity, while increasing PE consumption relative to the direct electrification pathway. Material trade-offs also emerge, with reduced pressure on some battery-related materials but increased demand for platinum and iridium, potentially exceeding the corresponding reserve benchmarks. Demand-side sufficiency substantially alleviates these pressures, delivering the strongest reductions in total energy demand and emissions while requiring lower infrastructure deployment requirements.

Numerical evaluation of a complex fenestration system with solar optics and photovoltaic cells for building energy efficiency and daylight autonomy
abstract: Dielectric crossed compound parabolic concentrator-photovoltaic (CCPC-PV) windows represent an attractive building-integrated photovoltaic (BIPV) fenestration solution, capable of harvesting solar energy for electricity generation while admitting daylight into occupied spaces. Nevertheless, conventional whole-building simulation tools cannot natively reproduce the complex optical, thermal, and electrical behaviours of CCPC-PV windows, and holistic building-scale evaluations considering diverse window design scenarios and climatic conditions remain insufficient. This study presents a coupled multi-physics simulation workflow based on the Equivalent Layer Fenestration Model (ELFM). It converts ray-tracing and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) outputs of complex CCPC-PV window geometry into equivalent-layer thermal/optical datasets compatible with EnergyPlus. Parametric simulations are conducted across different concentrator spacing layouts, window-to-wall ratios (WWRs), and climatic conditions. The simulation results reveal that densely arranged CCPC-PV configurations deliver the best overall system performance. At WWR = 64%, the optimal layout achieves net energy savings of 56.86% in London, 67.63% in Barcelona, and 33.93% in Stockholm. Under all simulated conditions, CCPC-PV windows achieve higher useful daylight illuminance (UDI 500-2000 ) than conventional double-glazed windows and mitigate visual discomfort due to over-illumination. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of the coupled simulation framework for evaluating complex BIPV fenestration systems, and quantifies the energy and daylight benefits of CCPC-PV windows across different design and climate contexts.

Spillover effects and transmission channels of carbon price volatility
abstract: abstract Studies have shown that carbon markets influence financial markets, commodity prices, and overall uncertainty. However, the impacts of carbon price volatility on these areas remain underexplored. This study addresses this gap by analyzing the relationships between carbon price volatility, renewable energy assets, financial volatility, uncertainty, financial markets, and oil markets using weekly data, Vector Autoregressive and Global Vector Autoregressive models, and Granger causality tests. The shock identification assumes that carbon price volatility spreads through financial markets and uncertainty, eventually affecting oil markets. The results indicate that a carbon price volatility shock is potentially linked to increased financial volatility and uncertainty, while corresponding to declines in stock market performance for two to four weeks. After this period, the shock's effect dissipates. The variance decomposition reveals that carbon price volatility has a greater influence on volatility and uncertainty than on spot prices: carbon price volatility does not directly impact oil prices; instead, it affects only oil price volatility. The estimates also show that the potential primary drivers of carbon price volatility are renewable energy assets and financial volatility. These findings highlight (i) the spillover effects of carbon price volatility on financial markets, uncertainty, and oil markets, (ii) the potential transmission channels of carbon price volatility, and (iii) the connectedness of carbon price volatility with volatility indices, where higher carbon price volatility is associated with greater volatility in financial and oil markets.

title: Beyond daily average irradiance: Instantaneous homogeneous light distribution unlocks higher productivity in fixed-tilt agrivoltaics
Comparative assessment of three all-sky photometry systems for the local characterization of daylight climates
abstract: Characterizing the angular distribution of sky luminance is crucial for solar applications; however, traditional sky-scanner technology presents important limitations that motivate the use of alternative instrumentation. This study evaluates the sensitivity of sky-type classification to alternative instrumentation (a high dynamic range imaging system and a photodiode array) and how consistent they are compared to sky-scanners regarding the measurement of local solar radiation patterns. A methodology was developed to determine sky type from the measurements of alternative instruments, and the instrument potential to obtain results comparable to that of sky-scanners was assessed under various sky conditions. For sky characterization, the Tregenza method was applied to all three instruments; however, given the significant differences among the luminance detectors, differing data processing pipelines were employed. Results indicate that the assessed instruments are suitable for sky classification, but the imaging system exhibited the most balanced statistics. Particularly, under clear-sky conditions the other instruments showed greater uncertainty, which is interpreted as higher deviation from theoretical sky classes. The assessment suggests that full-sky imaging presents lower RMS values and more classification stability under the evaluated experimental conditions, which encompass a single location and a temporal period limited to three months during spring-summer season.

title: Machine learning approaches in solar forecasting across different climate types: A unified evaluation framework
abstract: With the continuous development of solar energy technology, solar forecasting has become increasingly important. Accurate short-term solar forecasting could help maintain grid stability and provide reliable power. It is also critical for scheduling in intra-day electricity markets and grid operations. Compared to Deep Learning models, Machine Learning models offer the advantages of faster computation and better adaptability to small datasets. However, there is a lack of a unified evaluation framework to evaluate Machine Learning models due to the diversity of datasets, time step, forecasting horizon, set up and evaluation metrics. This work addresses this gap by evaluating six validated Machine Learning methods including Linear Regression, Polynomial Regression, Support Vector Regression, Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting and Artificial Neural Network for hourly solar irradiance forecasting across five different geographical regions: Canberra, Shanghai, Miami, Amherst and Kitakyushu. Results reveal that all Machine Learning models outperform the Smart Persistence Model (SPM) at the one-hour horizon; tree-ensemble methods, specifically Random Forest (RF) and XGBoost, achieve the highest overall accuracy and provide predictive performance competitive with DL models at the one-hour-ahead horizon. In stable-sky locations such as Canberra, the RF model achieved a normalized Root Mean Square Error (nRMSE) of 48.97% and a coefficient of determination ( R 2 ) of 0.8859, whereas the nRMSE increased to 61.47% in the highly variable conditions of Kitakyushu. This work helps establish a consistent framework for future studies, facilitating better comparison and improvement of Machine Learning models in solar forecasting.

Numerical and experimental investigation of heat transfer in photothermal liquid films for parametric analysis of their applicability in photovoltaic-thermal (PV/T) systems
abstract: Falling-film cooling for photovoltaic (PV) systems is employed in warm climates to boost electrical efficiency. However, few studies have addressed thermal energy recovery from PV panels by recycling liquid films over their surface. In this paper, experiments involving thin liquid film cooling a sun-heated surface were conducted, along with a numerical investigation of heat transfer between the liquid film, the surrounding air, and a PV panel. The liquid film was modeled using the volume-of-fluid (VOF) approach and numerical simulations were performed to parametrically analyze film cooling as a foundation for a simplified photovoltaic-thermal (PV/T) concept. Several PV cooling scenarios were examined. For the investigated open falling-film configuration, water exhibited low thermal performance, below 50%, due to evaporation. In contrast, a heat-transfer fluid with reduced evaporation (40 °C, 1 bar) is an interesting alternative to water. Although limited by other operational characteristics, a simulated organic oil exhibited 71% total efficiency.

Multistage stochastic bidding of hydrogen-enabled virtual power plants with off-taker commitments
abstract: Hydrogen refuelling stations equipped with on-site renewable generation, electrolysers, hydrogen storage and optional reconversion can operate as hydrogen-enabled virtual power plants, arbitraging across electricity markets while meeting contracted hydrogen demand. This paper proposes a multistage stochastic mixed-integer linear program to co-optimise hydrogen procurement with day-ahead bidding and sequential recourse in reserve, intraday and imbalance markets. The model represents electrolyser and fuel cell on, standby, and off states, warm and cold starts, and degradation, while battery ageing is captured through cycle-dependent costs. A case study with real-world data compares four portfolios built around a photovoltaic-driven station: fuel cell with reserve, no reserve, battery replacing the fuel cell, and optional hydrogen sales. Results show that reserve remuneration is the main profitability driver and materially reshapes operating states. The fuel cell rarely generates electricity and is used mainly to support reserve provision, whereas the electrolyser concentrates production to limit starts and degradation. Replacing the fuel cell with a battery provides the strongest profit uplift, while hydrogen sales deliver a smaller, episodic benefit.

title: Process-based Monte Carlo cost simulation for offshore wind farm decommissioning: A scenario analysis for the German North Sea
abstract: : We estimate the probability distribution of the net costs of decommissioning a first-generation offshore wind farm in the German North Sea. The process-based Monte Carlo model covers a 288 MW reference wind farm with 80 monopile-founded 3.6 MW turbines and ten scenarios. The model is based on expert judgments and market data from a multi-year research project with industry partners. It models dependence among cost rates and among process durations and quantities. It links offshore removal to onshore processing costs and material revenues. Expected net costs, defined as gross expenditures less material revenues, range from €242,000 to €545,000 per MW in 2022 prices. Correlation among inputs raises the upper tail far more than the mean. The 95th percentile of the baseline lies 34% above the mean, versus 23% for independent inputs. The decommissioning concepts filed with the German regulator include risk surcharges of up to 30%. Such a surcharge covers the 95th percentile only for independent inputs. Material revenues fall short of onshore costs in 15% of the baseline simulations. Leaving the scour protection in situ lowers expected costs by 18%, and cutting the foundation above the seabed lowers them by a further 9 percentage points. Feeder logistics raise costs by 48% for foundations and by 65% for foundations and turbines, conditional on the fleet, the 2022 vessel market, and the implicit treatment of weather. For the 3.6 MW reference case, the scenario ranking is the same under all stochastic specifications tested. The results provide a benchmark for financial provisioning.

title: Performance investigation of a novel valve-integrated ejector-enhanced CO2 cycle for heating and cooling
Experimental investigation of a multi-buoy cooperative point-absorber wave energy
abstract: This study presents a proof-of-concept experimental investigation of a multi-buoy cooperative point-absorber wave energy converter (WEC). The proposed concept consists of an array of surface-penetrating buoys connected through a shared closed-loop hydraulic power take-off (PTO) system. Energy is extracted through the collective motion of the buoy array, where pressurised flow generated by individual buoys drives a turbine within the hydraulic circuit. A 1:40 scale model was tested in the wave tank facilities at the University of Oslo. Experiments with regular and irregular long-crested waves at two different incident angles were conducted to assess power absorption, wave period response, and interaction effects. Two array configurations were investigated: an eight-buoy array with an axis-to-axis spacing of 1.5 buoy diameters, and a four-buoy array with a 3.0 diameter spacing. Although piston head leakage affected the power measurements, our results demonstrate that the WEC absorbs incoming wave energy and produces measurable power. The eight-buoy configuration achieved the highest power output per buoy compared to the four-buoy configuration, but exhibited increased sensitivity to wave period and wave heading, due to buoy-buoy interactions, such as collisions. This study highlights buoy count and internal buoy spacing as key design parameters for cooperative point-absorber wave energy systems. The results indicate that higher buoy counts enhance hydraulic cooperation, and increased buoy spacing improves robustness to wave heading and reduces destructive interaction effects. We also suggest that a lower system inertia can improve responsiveness to shorter waves. These insights provide a foundation for further optimisation and future full-scale development.

Mapping Colombia's green hydrogen potential: A nationwide geospatial suitability and cost screening assessment
abstract: This study develops a comprehensive geospatial framework to identify and evaluate suitable locations for green hydrogen production in Colombia, integrating renewable energy potential, infrastructure readiness, and environmental constraints. The framework combines high-resolution Geographic Information System (GIS) modeling with a screening-level cost assessment of Levelized Costs of Electricity (LCOE) and Hydrogen (LCOH), applied to solar PV, onshore wind, and offshore wind technologies. Results reveal that approximately 5.1% of Colombia’s land area is eligible for solar PV, 1% for onshore wind, and 2.1% of its maritime Exclusive Economic Zone for offshore wind once environmental, technical, and legal restrictions are applied. Among the assessed regions, La Guajira emerges as the most promising hub, achieving LCOE values as low as 41 $/MWh for onshore wind and corresponding LCOH values of 6–8 $/kg. The study applies an oversizing factor methodology for renewable–electrolyzer systems, adapted from and consistent with previous studies, improving accuracy compared with conventional 1:1 capacity assumptions. Sensitivity analysis shows that renewable-resource utilization and electrolyzer specific electricity consumption are major technical drivers of LCOH, while the dominant economic drivers vary across renewable pathways. Institutional barriers, such as land-use restrictions under ANH concessions and grid infrastructure gaps, remain key bottlenecks. The findings inform policy design, investment prioritization, and spatial planning for Colombia’s Green Hydrogen Roadmap and provide a replicable framework for other emerging economies pursuing renewable-based hydrogen strategies.

Thermal analysis of a ground-mounted photovoltaic system coupled with the crop of a metal-hyperaccumulating plant using multiple modelling approaches
abstract: Understanding the operating temperature of photovoltaic (PV) modules is crucial for assessing their electrical performance, yet most agrivoltaic models focus on crop yield rather than PV thermal behaviour. This study addresses this gap by proposing a one-dimensional dynamic thermal model based on a nodal approach to simulate the PV modules’ temperatures. The model was validated using PV back-surface temperatures measured during a two-year experiment and integrate soil and vegetation surface temperatures and meteorological parameters. This model (Model 3) was evaluated against two simplified thermal models: the Ross thermal model (Model 1) and the Normal Operating Cell Temperature model (Model 2). Model 3 showed the greatest precision with a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) down to 1.6°C and a Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency coefficient (NSE) > 92 %, outperforming Models 1 and 2 by 20 % in NSE and 50-80 % in RMSE reduction. Model 1 performed better under cloudy conditions (RMSE 3.6-4.5°C; NSE 72-80 %), while Model 2 slightly improved sunny-day predictions (NSE up to 82 %). Model 3 consistently provided the best results (NSE > 92 %). Comparing simulated and measured electrical energy production of an opaque module, Models 1 and 2 overestimated output (+2 % to +3 %, more under sunny conditions), while Model 3 exhibited the closest agreement (deviation < 1 %). Parametric simulations with Model 3 also highlighted the potential of brownfield sites in southern France for ecovoltaic deployment. This work provides a robust thermal modelling framework for ecovoltaic systems, improving performance predictions and supporting sustainable energy integration.
